name: room
text: Room opened — goal: accessibility: Make EXCAVA usable by EVERYONE — contrast, mobile/touch, reduced-motion, keyboard nav, scr

name: Ramp
text: Add a single, high-contrast focus ring that follows tab order—no exceptions. This ensures keyboard users always see where they are, which is critical for people who rely on keyboards or switch devices. The trade-off is visual clutter for sighted mouse users, but that’s minor compared to the accessibility win.

name: Reader
text: The single high-contrast ring still risks obscuring critical content on dense screens—users with low vision or cognitive load may struggle to parse both focus and content. A better alternative is a subtle, non-intrusive ring that only appears on long-press or delayed hover, paired with a keyboard-only toggle for sighted users who prefer minimal distraction. Settle it with user testing: measure task completion time and error rates for both sighted keyboard users and low-vision users across dense and sparse screens.

name: Ramp
text:
Keep the single, high-contrast focus ring that moves with tab order—no exceptions. It’s the only way to guarantee every keyboard user can navigate without guessing where they are, which is non-negotiable for access. The trade-off is that sighted mouse users might briefly notice a ring, but that’s a minor visual hiccup compared to the barrier it removes. No other solution gives the same certainty for all users, all the time.

name: Reader
text: The single high-contrast ring fails sighted keyboard users with cognitive load or low vision when it obscures dense content—it’s not just a "brief" distraction, it’s a barrier. A better alternative is a keyboard-only focus indicator that scales with content density, paired with a persistent but subtle ring for mouse users; settle it with a live test where three low-vision participants confirm they can complete a task without losing context.

name: Access
text: DECISION: Ship a semi-transparent, high-contrast focus ring with adjustable opacity that scales with content density, allowing keyboard users to navigate while minimizing visual clutter for sighted users. This result must deliver a usable interface for everyone, and the lead developer owns the artifact, ensuring it meets accessibility standards and is thoroughly tested with screen readers and keyboard navigation.
